definition: The two starting assumptions of special relativity: the laws of physics are the same in every inertial reference frame, and every inertial observer measures the speed of light in a vacuum as $c$, whatever the motion of the source.

The equations $x' = \gamma(x - vt)$ and $t' = \gamma(t - vx/c^{2})$ that convert an event's position and time from one inertial frame to another moving at velocity $v$ relative to it; they reduce to the Galilean equations when $v$ is much less than $c$.
$\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}$ for two inertial frames with relative speed $v$; it is never less than 1, equals 1 only when $v = 0$, and grows without limit as $v$ approaches $c$.

The rule $u' = (u - v)/(1 - uv/c^{2})$ for an object's velocity $u'$ in a frame moving at $v$, when the object has velocity $u$ in the original frame; for speeds below $c$ it never gives a result of $c$ or more.
The quantity $\Delta s$ between two events, given by $(\Delta s)^{2} = (c\Delta t)^{2} - (\Delta x)^{2}$; it has the same value in every inertial frame, even though $\Delta t$ and $\Delta x$ do not.
